details:
**Kitty Genovese**
A bar manager who was stabbed to death by Winston Moseley outside her apartment in Kew Gardens, Queens, New York, in March 1964. Her murder is the most famous example of the bystander effect and inspired research on it, so the phenomenon is sometimes called the "Genovese effect" or "Genovese syndrome."

**Thirty-eight witnesses**
The New York Times famously reported that 38 neighbors watched or heard the Genovese attack without calling for help. Later investigations showed this account was greatly exaggerated: far fewer people actually saw the attack, and at least one person did call the police, so the case is now considered an erroneous or misleading example of the effect.

**Smoke-filled room experiment**
A classic 1968 experiment by Latané and Darley in which Columbia University students filled out a questionnaire while smoke slowly poured into the room through a vent. Participants who were alone usually reported the smoke quickly, while those sitting with passive confederates often did not report it at all.

**John Darley and Bibb Latané**
The social psychologists who first described and studied the bystander effect in the laboratory, partly in response to the Genovese murder. Their experiments and their book The Unresponsive Bystander: Why Doesn't He Help? (1970) proposed a decision model of helping in emergencies.

**Diffusion of responsibility**
A key explanation for the bystander effect proposed by Darley and Latané: when many people witness an emergency, each feels less personal responsibility to act, assuming that someone else will help.

**Seizure (intercom) experiment**
A 1968 study by Darley and Latané in which participants talking over an intercom from separate booths, with microphones switched on one at a time, heard another "participant" (actually a recording) apparently have an epileptic seizure. The more people subjects believed were listening, the less likely and slower they were to seek help.

**Good Samaritan laws**
Laws that protect people from liability when they help someone in an emergency, and in some places require bystanders to give reasonable assistance. They are meant to counteract the bystander effect.

**Pluralistic ignorance**
A cause of the bystander effect in which each person in an ambiguous situation looks to others for cues; seeing no one else react, everyone concludes that help is not needed. Together with diffusion of responsibility and social influence, it explains why larger groups help less.

**Wang Yue**
A two-year-old girl in Foshan, China, who was run over by vehicles in 2011 and ignored by many passersby, as captured on surveillance video. The case caused national outrage and prompted Chinese debate over and adoption of Good Samaritan laws.

**Liquor store theft**
A field experiment by Latané and Darley's research group in which staged thefts, including a case of beer being stolen from a liquor store, occurred while customers were present. Customers were less likely to report the theft when other people were also present.

**Ringelmann effect and social loafing**
The Ringelmann effect, found by French engineer Max Ringelmann in rope-pulling experiments, is the tendency for individuals to exert less effort as group size increases. This "social loafing" is closely related to the diffusion of responsibility that underlies the bystander effect.

**Richard Philpot's CCTV study**
A 2019 study led by Richard Philpot that analyzed surveillance footage of real public conflicts in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and South Africa. It found that at least one bystander intervened in about 90 percent of cases, and that intervention became more likely as the number of bystanders grew, challenging the classic view of the effect.

**P. M. Markey's chat room study**
A 2000 study by Patrick Markey that applied the bystander framework to online chat rooms, posing as users with names such as "Suzy Harmen" and "Jake Harmen" to request help. Responses were slower in groups with more people, but addressing a specific person by name eliminated the effect.

**Marco van Bommel's reversal**
A study by Marco van Bommel and colleagues showing that the bystander effect can be reversed online when people are made more self-aware, for example by highlighting their names in red (the "salient" condition). Under these conditions, the presence of others actually increased helping.

**What Would You Do?**
An ABC hidden-camera television show hosted by John Quiñones that stages public scenarios, such as harassment or theft, to see whether bystanders will intervene.
